title: Sartorius v. Siouxlands Presbytery
disposition_detail: The SJC denied TE Arthur Sartorius's complaint, leaving Siouxlands Presbytery's not-guilty verdicts undisturbed and declining to reverse, annul, or remand for retrial; it held the complainant did not show trial-court error.
first_summary: Did Siouxlands Presbytery fail its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by finding TE Lawrence not guilty? The SJC denied the complaint. It held that a complaint against a not-guilty verdict cannot trigger a superior-court retrial; under BCO 43 the superior court may only annul or remand, not reverse. The complainant did not meet his burden to show error from the record, which included defense testimony and Defense Exhibit 1 sufficient to defer to the trial court. The SJC did not decide Lawrence's actual views.
summary: Did a presbytery fail in its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by acquitting a minister on theological-error charges? The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the acquittal undisturbed. A complaint against a not-guilty verdict cannot provoke a retrial at the superior court; under BCO 43 the superior court may only annul or remand, not reverse, and the complainant bore the burden to show error from the record. The record contained the defendant's testimony, including recantations or clarifications, Defense Exhibit 1, and witness testimony sufficient to refrain from contradicting the trial court. The SJC expressly did not decide the defendant's actual views. A separate concurrence elaborated deference standards but did not change the judgment.

sources.supports: Adopted SJC decision on complaint, issue, judgment, reasoning, vote, and separate concurring opinion.

evidence_notes.identity_and_adoption: Case 2016-16, Sartorius v. Siouxlands Presbytery; SJC decision on complaint dated Oct. 19, 2017, adopted by roll call 22–1 with Fowler dissenting (lines 13, 237–239). RE Donahoe's concurrence at lines 241–245 is a separate opinion.
evidence_notes.dispute: Sartorius complained that Siouxlands Presbytery failed its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by finding TE Lawrence not guilty at Trial 2; the SJC framed the issue at lines 193–195. Trial 2 acquittals appear at lines 155–177, and Presbytery's denial of the complaint appears at line 185.
evidence_notes.outcomes_and_reasons: Judgment: 'No. The Complaint is denied' (lines 197–199). The SJC reasoned that a complaint against a verdict cannot provoke a superior-court retrial, that under BCO 43 the superior court may only annul or remand rather than reverse, and that complainant did not meet his burden to show error from the record (lines 203–220).
evidence_notes.qualifications: The adopted decision expressly said it did not comment on the defendant's actual views in relation to the Constitution, only that complainant did not demonstrate trial-court error (lines 217–220). The Donahoe concurrence discusses deference and acquittal-complaint due process but is not adopted reasoning (lines 241–253, 327–395, 736–779).
evidence_notes.incorporated_decisions: Prior matters are summarized as procedural history: Case 2008-14 White v. Siouxlands sustained a complaint and ordered a BCO 31-2 investigation (lines 69, 263); Case 2012-08 Sartorius v. Siouxlands sustained a complaint in part for procedural error and remanded for a new trial with instructions (lines 133–149, 270–281). The current decision does not adopt their merits as its own holding.

source_limits: The supplied source contains the SJC decision and a lengthy separate concurrence, but not the full trial record, transcripts, briefs, or the complete prior decisions. The concurrence is not adopted reasoning and cannot supply the SJC's holding.
benchmark_examples: C01: preserve mixed procedural outcomes and the unsuccessful requested relief; here the complaint was denied and no retrial was ordered.
C20: an unexplained disposition should remain unexplained; here the SJC did supply its denial rationale.
